thread.title_full: Southern California woman fears missing dog was taken by mountain lion amid warnings for pet owners - NewsBreak

author: Peter Rubinstein
title: Southern California woman fears missing dog was taken by mountain lion amid warnings for pet owners - NewsBreak
text:
By Peter Rubinstein ,
1 hours ago A Southern California community has expressed increasing concern about a possible uptick in mountain lion attacks after one resident said their dog went missing over the weekend, leaving behind only a trail of blood.
A resident in Oak Glen, located in San Bernardino County, said this week that she believes her mastiff was attacked and dragged off by a mountain lion, according to KTLA. She said she found a trail of blood but not her dog, which she said typically returns home after roaming the neighborhood.
Gianna Sedillo, 17, a neighbor of the dog owner, said that their community has encountered many bears, coyotes and deer in the area. “You just have to keep an eye on your animals, especially with this wildlife,” she said. “You never know what’s going to happen.”

• Woman plunges to her death from Carnival cruise balcony off California coast
Sedillo told KTLA that other mountain lion attacks in nearby neighborhoods have put Oak Glen residents on high alert.
“I do have a little taser I carry around with me when I go out to take care of my animals,” she said. “We always try to lock them up at night.”
Last weekend, a mountain lion killed two dogs at a San Bernardino County house while owners Laurie and Roger Schultz were out of town.
Though attacks typically occur at night, the rare daytime incident prompted an official with the California Department of Fish and Wildlife to recommend safety precautions to California residents concerned about their own pets.
"The department recommends residents take preventative measures to protect their pets and livestock from predators," a CDFW spokesperson said in a statement after the incident in Yucaipa.
"Some steps residents can take are supervising pets when outdoors, especially at night, and providing a secure enclosure for pets that are outside," the spokesperson said.
California is home to thousands of mountain lions, a protected species typically found in mountainous areas and known for being solitary, though territorial, predators with little interest in interacting with humans.
But given the chance, mountain lions will attack pet dogs and cats, particularly if they can reach them when their owners are not present.
The CDFW said that it would be investigating the mauling incident to ensure it is not part of a larger pattern.
The attack occurred Saturday when the Schultzes were away. The couple was monitoring their dogs, Summer, a 65-pound Anatolian Shepherd, and Winter, a 90-pound Siberian Husky, through a live camera installed in their backyard.
Roger Schultz last saw his dogs inside their indoor-outdoor enclosure before the mountain lion attacked.
He said he checked the live stream camera several times and believed the dogs were sleeping. Hours later, however, the couple grew concerned and asked a neighbor to check on their home.
"A couple hours later I checked again and said, 'Wait a minute they're not moving,'" he told ABC7. "I called the neighbor, asked him to come up and check. He was like, 'Dude, they are mauled seriously.'"
Roger Schultz tracked the deceased dog using a receiver on its collar as the mountain lion dragged it to its den about 150 yards behind his home. And though he and his wife are mourning the loss of their dogs, he told reporters that his main worry is for the safety of other family pets and children in the neighborhood.
Though mountain lions prefer to avoid humans, they are still "opportunistic" predators who will seldom pass up the chance to hunt smaller animals. "They're opportunistic. They will take pets. They will take cats, they will take dogs," CDFW information officer Peter Tira told the Mirror US.
